summary: When a device moves between networks, finding out whether it is on a new network and getting a working IPv4 setup can take a noticeable amount of time. This document collects steps drawn from experience with ARP, DHCP and IPv4 link-local addresses into Detecting Network Attachment for IPv4 (DNAv4), to cut that delay. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: When you walk into a new room, you quickly check if it is the same room or a new one, so you do not waste time asking everyone who you are again.

questions: how to reduce handover delay in ipv4
how does a host detect network attachment
why use unicast arp instead of broadcast
subtitle: A quick unicast ARP check that lets a host confirm it is back on a known network without redoing DHCP.

tldr.problem: Detecting that a host has moved to another network and obtaining or keeping an IPv4 configuration can take a significant share of the total handover time. Address conflict detection alone can take as much as seven seconds.
tldr.mechanism: The host remembers each network's test nodes (preferably routers) and its lease, then sends a unicast ARP Request to a test node. A matching ARP Reply confirms the old configuration is still valid, while DHCP runs in parallel.
tldr.outcome: On a previously visited LAN, re-attachment can take a few milliseconds. It is only an optimization: it must never give a false positive, and a missed match merely falls back to normal DHCP.

facts.label: Procedure frequency
facts.value: no more than once a second (RECOMMENDED)

today: RFC 4436 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Handover Is Slow
sections.content:
When a host switches between points of attachment, the time to notice the move and to get (or keep) a working IPv4 configuration may be a large fraction of the total handover latency. Detecting Network Attachment for IPv4 (DNAv4) combines lessons from deploying ARP, DHCP and IPv4 Link-Local addresses to cut that time.

When DHCP gives a new address, the client SHOULD use ARP to check that the address is not already in use. This address conflict detection can take as much as seven seconds. Shortening it would raise the risk of address conflicts. When a client simply re-validates an old address with the DHCP INIT-REBOOT mechanism, conflict detection is not required, but the server may be slow or down.
sections.eli5: Joining a network normally means a lot of waiting to make sure nobody else is using your address. If you were here before, that waiting is mostly wasted.

sections.title: Design Principles of DNAv4
sections.content:
DNAv4 targets a host that holds a DHCP address it has not released, with time still left on the lease. It sends a unicast ARP Request to a router previously known on that link. Unicast is gentler than broadcast, especially on 802.11 networks where broadcasts may go out at rates as low as 1 Mb/sec. If the host is on the wrong link, a unicast to an absent router's MAC address harmlessly disappears, whereas a broadcast could pollute ARP caches or disrupt a device legitimately using the same private address.

The RFC draws several conclusions:

  • DNAv4 is a performance optimization, so false positives are not acceptable.
  • False negatives are acceptable. If a router ignores unicast ARP Requests, the host just works as it did without DNAv4.
  • Where it fails, it should add little or no delay, so DHCP proceeds in parallel.
  • Trials are cheap: an ARP packet on Ethernet is just 42 octets, so trying all candidate configurations is often best.
  • To enable low latency handoffs it needs to complete in less than 10 ms.

Because it depends on ARP, it is not suitable for media that do not support ARP.
sections.eli5: The host quietly knocks on one familiar door. If the right person answers, it is home. If nobody answers, nothing is lost and it does things the slow way.

sections.title: The Reachability Test
sections.content:
On a "Link Up" indication, the host saves, for each network, the IPv4 and MAC address of one or more test nodes plus its IPv4 configuration (DHCP client identifier, assigned address and lease expiration). It SHOULD use local routers, preferably default gateways, as test nodes, and may test several in parallel. It SHOULD only configure routes whose next hop passes the test.

The test is skipped if the host has no operable routable address on that network, knows no test nodes, uses DHCP authentication (RFC 3118), or would present a different DHCP Client Identifier than the one used for that configuration.

If a DHCPv4 client is operational, it is RECOMMENDED to run DHCP in parallel and use the first answer. If DHCP later returns a different result, the host SHOULD abandon the test result and use DHCP, unless the confirmed address was manually assigned. Without a reply there is little value in aggressive retransmission: it is RECOMMENDED to retransmit no more than twice, and to run DNAv4 no more than once a second.
sections.eli5: The host keeps a note for each place it has been: who to knock on and what address it had. It knocks while also asking the normal way, and takes whichever answer comes first.

sections.title: The ARP Request and Its Rules
sections.content:
The test is a unicast ARP Request. The host MUST set ar$tpa to the IPv4 address of the node being tested and ar$spa to its own candidate address. The request MUST use the host MAC address as source and the test node MAC address as destination. The host puts its MAC address in ar$sha and sets ar$tha to 0.

A valid ARP Reply must match: its ar$sha must equal the MAC address the host aimed at, and its ar$spa must equal the ar$tpa of the Request. On a match the host keeps using its address, subject to lease behavior in RFC 2131.

Until the configuration is confirmed, the host SHOULD NOT respond to ARP Requests and SHOULD NOT broadcast ARP Requests with its address in ar$spa. An ICMP Echo Request (RFC 792) SHOULD NOT be used as a substitute, because it needs ARP first and a reply can come from the wrong network or an off-link router if the MAC address is not checked.
sections.eli5: The knock is addressed to one specific mailbox. The host only believes it is home if the answer comes from that exact mailbox and carries the right address.

sections.title: Falling Back to DHCP and Link-Local Addresses
sections.content:
If the host has an operable routable address on some network and DHCPv4 is enabled, it SHOULD enter INIT-REBOOT and broadcast a DHCPREQUEST in parallel with the tests. The request goes to the broadcast address because a unicast one could not be routed back if the client moved subnets. With no operable address, it enters INIT and broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER. With the Rapid Commit Option (RFC 4039) this can shrink from a 4-message to a 2-message exchange.

DNAv4 applies only to addresses with a lease. IPv4 Link-Local addresses (RFC 3927) have no guaranteed lifetime, so a host reclaiming one MUST perform full probing and announcement and MUST NOT use DNAv4 as a shortcut. Manually assigned addresses may be treated as having an infinite lifetime, but DNAv4 SHOULD NOT be enabled for them by default, and they need more aggressive retransmission.
sections.eli5: If the quick check fails, the host just asks the usual way. Addresses that were never officially lent to it must still be claimed the slow, careful way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DNAv4 inherits the vulnerabilities of ARP and DHCP. ARP traffic is not secured, so an attacker on the network can spoof a reply to the reachability test and make the host believe it is attached to a network it is not. Unsecured DHCPv4 lets an attacker pose as a server for the same purpose (see RFC 3118).

The effect is typically limited to denial of service, unless the host uses its configuration for other purposes. For example, a host that disables its personal firewall because it believes it is on a home network could be compromised. Adjusting security configuration based on DNAv4 is NOT RECOMMENDED, and hosts that depend on secure IP configuration SHOULD NOT use DNAv4.
sections.eli5: A trickster could fake the friendly answer and fool the host into thinking it is home. So the host should not lower its guard just because the check passed.
